title: Steam Families: Why a Shared Game Is Missing or Already in Use
description: Separate game eligibility, available copies, account ownership and installation problems before buying another copy or changing family settings.
intro: A game missing from a Steam Family is not automatically an installation fault. First separate three questions: is this game eligible to be shared, does the family own an available copy, and is the correct account trying to launch it? Reinstalling a game cannot solve every licence problem.

sources.name: Valve: Steam Families User Guide & FAQ
Valve Steamworks: Steam Families and shared licences

diagrams.title: A missing game has three different checks
diagrams.foot: Diagnose the licence before reinstalling the game.

sections: Start with the symptom, not a repair utility

Write down what happens before changing anything. A title absent from the shared library, a message saying that no copy is available, and a game that launches then crashes are different incidents. Capture the exact wording and the point at which it appears. Note the game name and edition, because a base game, an expansion and a free-to-play item may not have the same sharing behaviour. This short description is more useful than a general statement that sharing is broken. It also stops you repeating unrelated troubleshooting steps while the underlying question remains a licence or eligibility issue.
Check whether the title is shareable

Valve's family FAQ lists exclusions including publisher opt-outs, some third-party account or subscription requirements, region restrictions, unsupported operating systems and games marked private by their owner. Free-to-play games and their purchased DLC are also listed among content that cannot be shared. The presence of a game in one person's library therefore does not establish that another family member can use it. Check the exact title in the current Steam client and consult its official support information. Avoid third-party lists that do not distinguish the present Steam Families system from older sharing arrangements or that describe a different edition.
Count copies of the game, rather than family members

Valve illustrates shared access with a family owning one copy of a title: another member cannot use that same available copy simultaneously, while a different eligible game may still be playable. Owning an additional copy changes that particular copy count. The practical question is whether your family already has access to another copy before anyone spends money. Coordinate a short check with the other member and record whether the message changes when they finish. This is a diagnostic comparison, not a recommendation to purchase a second licence. A failed test does not prove that the publisher supports sharing or that the installation itself is healthy.
Ownership, installation and progress are separate things

Valve's developer documentation treats a shared family licence as temporary access rather than permanent ownership for the borrowing account. Installing files does not establish a separate purchase entitlement. Keep that distinction in mind when a launcher offers an installation button but a later step reports an access problem. Likewise, treat save data as a separate concern before deleting local folders or switching accounts. If the game has its own account, identify which account holds the relevant progress. Do not assume that a family relationship merges every external account, purchase history or saved character. Ask the game's official support team when that relationship is unclear.
Use a small comparison matrix

Choose one eligible game that you can already launch and compare it with the problem title on the same account and computer. Record whether each appears in the library, whether another member is playing it, and whether the failure occurs before the game starts. Keep the comparison small: changing the account, computer, network and game at the same time makes the result difficult to interpret. If the working title still works while the other fails, you have narrowed the investigation without proving a specific cause. If both fail, examine the shared account or client context before deciding that two unrelated installations are damaged.
Compare the edition named on the receipt

Before diagnosing an expansion, compare the full product names rather than only the artwork. Make a two-column note with the exact item shown in the owner's purchase history and the exact item another member is trying to launch. Record any separate launcher message alongside it. This does not prove which entitlement is required, but it gives official support a concrete comparison to inspect and prevents a mistaken purchase of an unrelated edition while the original access question remains unresolved.
Avoid disruptive changes as a first experiment

Do not leave a family, create a replacement group or buy a duplicate game just to see what happens. Membership rules and waiting periods deserve a careful read in Valve's current FAQ before a change. An account action can be harder to undo than restarting the client. Prefer recording the present state, checking entitlement and confirming which person owns the relevant copy. If files genuinely fail to launch after access is established, use our Steam launch troubleshooting checklist. That guide addresses the local failure path rather than attempting to override sharing restrictions or account permissions.
Send the evidence that support can actually use

A useful report contains the exact game and edition, a description of which account owns a copy, the error wording, the date and time of the attempt, and the result of the small comparison. Explain whether the title is absent entirely or visible but unavailable. Include a cropped screenshot only after removing personal details. Never send a password, a Steam Guard code or a recovery code to a person claiming to fix sharing. Valve's official help portal is the appropriate starting point for account-specific cases. This guide organises the investigation; it does not certify that your household or a particular title qualifies for sharing.
What a successful check establishes

A successful launch demonstrates that this title worked on this account and device at the time of the check. It does not establish permanent eligibility, a new purchase or future availability. Keep the short notes until the issue is resolved, then use the same symptom categories if it returns. For readers preparing a trip, our offline preparation guide covers a different question: what to test before losing a network connection. Sharing eligibility and offline behaviour should be checked separately, without assuming that success in one proves the other.

title: Steam Game Recording: Keep the Clip You Need Without Filling Your Drive
description: Understand temporary background footage, saved clips and MP4 export, then test audio and storage with a short recording before a long session.
intro: A Steam recording visible on a timeline is not the same thing as an exported video file. Decide whether you want temporary background footage, a saved highlight or a file to share. Then test a short clip, including its audio, before relying on a long recording session.

sources.name: Valve: Steam Game Recording settings, storage and export FAQ

diagrams.title: Footage, clip and exported file
diagrams.foot: These are different stages; verify the exported file.

diagrams.title: A storage budget has several parts
cards: Files stored in a chosen folder
diagrams.foot: Check the real folders before deleting anything.

diagrams.title: Test the audio before the match
diagrams.foot: Play back a short local export before sharing.

sections: Choose the recording behaviour for the session

Valve documents two recording approaches: a background capture that keeps gameplay as you play, and on-demand recording started when you choose. Open Steam's Game Recording settings and review the current selection before an important session. A background option suits an unexpected highlight, while a planned demonstration may be easier to manage deliberately. Neither choice guarantees that a specific moment has already been preserved. Treat the first session as a rehearsal: make a brief recording, locate it, and inspect it before committing a whole evening. That small test gives you a concrete result on your own setup rather than relying on a generic performance claim.
Understand what the temporary buffer can overwrite

According to Valve's FAQ, background recording has a configurable storage allowance and older temporary footage is overwritten as the allowance fills. Saving a clip is the step that retains a selected moment. After something important happens, make and check the clip promptly rather than assuming the rolling recording will remain indefinitely. Separate the existence of a timeline entry from your intention to keep it. If the moment matters, locate the saved item and play its beginning and end. This is particularly useful after a long session when several similar matches or attempts are easy to confuse and the timestamp alone may not identify the right sequence.
Check the exported file, not just the editor preview

Valve distinguishes its recording format and timeline from an exported MP4 video. If your goal is to send a file to someone, select the relevant clip and use the available export workflow. Then inspect the resulting file from its destination folder. Check that it opens in a normal video player, contains the expected beginning and end, and includes the intended sound. A successful preview inside Steam does not by itself establish that an export completed or that you selected the correct destination. Name the file meaningfully so you can distinguish a final clip from an earlier test without reopening every video.
Keep a small storage inventory

Write down the recording location configured in Steam and the folder used for your exports. Before a large cleanup, compare the files actually present with the clips you want to preserve. Saved clips and exported videos deserve attention in addition to the background allowance. Do not assume that one setting describes every video file elsewhere on the drive. If space is tight, move or remove only items you have identified and no longer need, after checking any copy you intend to keep. Avoid deleting an entire unfamiliar folder because a search result labels it a cache; its contents may include material you expected to retain.
Audio deserves its own rehearsal

Valve explains that gameplay capture can include audio from other programs when configured to do so. Before sharing, consider whether private voice chat, a notification or another person's conversation could be included. Make a short test with the same audio sources you expect to use, then listen to the exported result. Tell other participants when their voices may be recorded and respect their preferences. A video can look correct while its audio makes it unsuitable to publish. Check for silence, missing game sound and an unexpectedly loud microphone as separate observations; changing several audio options at once makes it harder to identify which setting mattered.
Use one clip as an export rehearsal

Choose a short, unimportant moment for the rehearsal and export it to a folder you can identify. Open that file outside the recording viewer, then record its name and location. Try sending this test file through the same route you intend to use for the final highlight. Inspect the received copy if you can. This checks the full transfer path without risking an irreplaceable recording or spending a long session discovering that an export was saved somewhere unexpected.
Timeline markers are navigation aids

Steamworks documentation describes timeline integration that developers can use to identify gameplay moments. Such markers help find an event in supported games; they are not evidence that every game produces the same labels. If a recording has no useful markers, look for the moment by reviewing the timeline itself and use a short descriptive clip name afterward. Avoid diagnosing missing integration as a broken capture solely because another game's timeline looks different. For a reproducible support report, record the game name, the Steam client version and whether footage exists without the expected marker. Those details distinguish capture failure from a navigation or integration question.
Assess performance with a controlled comparison

This guide does not claim a measured frame-rate cost for your hardware. If recording appears to affect play, compare the same repeatable scene with recording enabled and disabled while keeping the other settings constant. Note the game, resolution, graphics settings and recording configuration. A built-in benchmark or a repeatable training area is more useful than comparing two unrelated online matches. Observe whether the problem is a visible hitch, reduced responsiveness, an audio issue or an export problem. Our frame-rate and stutter guide explains why those symptoms should not be collapsed into one average FPS number.
A final check before sharing a highlight

Open the actual exported file once more and confirm that it is the correct clip. Review the first and last frames, listen to the sound, check the filename and remove any unintended personal information before publishing. Keep a local copy until you know that a transfer completed. For a travel setup, consult our Steam offline preparation checklist separately: the ability to record gameplay does not establish that the game itself will start without a connection. The reliable result is a clip you have opened and reviewed, with a storage location you can find again.

title: Steam Offline Mode Before a Trip: Test the Game, the Login and the Save
description: Prepare Steam offline play before losing internet access, distinguish game requirements from client settings, and protect saves when reconnecting.
intro: Prepare Steam Offline Mode while you still have a reliable connection. Update and launch the games you intend to take, confirm that the client can enter Offline Mode, and test the result. A downloaded game or a single-player label alone does not prove that a particular title will start offline.

sources.name: Valve: Offline Mode setup and troubleshooting
Valve: Steam Cloud and synchronisation conflicts

diagrams.title: Before you lose the connection
diagrams.foot: A download alone does not prove offline play.

diagrams.title: Three separate offline questions
cards: Can this client enter Offline Mode?
Does this title need a connection?
diagrams.foot: Success in one check does not establish the others.

diagrams.title: When you reconnect
cards: Protect the progress you intend to keep
diagrams.foot: Do not choose a conflicting save without checking it.

sections: Make a travel list before changing settings

Choose the specific games you intend to play and identify the device that will travel with you. Test those titles on that device rather than relying on a result from another computer. Record whether each reaches its normal playable state, whether a launcher requests another sign-in, and whether the save you expect is available. A concise list exposes an unfinished installation or a forgotten account requirement while you can still address it. It also provides an alternative if one title needs online access. The aim is a realistic preparation check, not a promise that every game in your library can operate without a connection.
Follow Valve's client preparation sequence

Valve's Offline Mode instructions start with Steam online, saved login credentials, completed updates and a launch of the intended games before switching through the Steam menu. Review the current official instructions on your device, because settings labels can change. Complete the setup while a dependable connection is available. If a client or game asks for an update during the rehearsal, finish it and test again before travel. Do not treat the visible download percentage as the only condition. A first launch may still expose an installation step or another requirement that a quick look at the library would not reveal.
Separate client access from a game's own requirements

Offline Mode limits access to Steam features that need the network; it does not remove a game's independent online requirements. A launcher, service or multiplayer component may have its own conditions. Check the official information for the exact game and test the part you actually want to use. Reaching a title screen is a weaker observation than loading your intended single-player mode and save. If that mode asks for a connection, record the message instead of assuming that a client setting will override it. Use official support for clarification and avoid tools claiming to disable ownership checks or change another service's access rules.
Rehearse the conditions you will really have

After completing the official preparation, run a short offline session on the travel device. Confirm that the game opens, the expected controls work and the relevant save loads. Then close it normally and check that you can return to the same progress under the conditions you tested. This is a proposed preparation routine, not a report of a test of your account. A successful check is useful evidence for that setup and moment; it cannot establish how a future update or service change will behave. Repeat it after a material change to the installation rather than relying indefinitely on an old result.
Plan for a sign-in request without taking account risks

Valve states that if the client requires a login, it cannot be bypassed without going online. Deal with an unexpected sign-in prompt while you still have a safe connection and access to your legitimate authentication method. Do not share passwords, Steam Guard codes or recovery information with a person offering an offline unlock. If you travel with several devices, keep their preparation separate and note which one has been tested. A rushed account change at a station or airport can create more uncertainty than it resolves. When preparation fails, taking another game that passes your check is often a more practical choice than relying on an unverified workaround.
Keep a preparation note you can use without a network

For each selected title, record the device, the date, the mode you opened and the save you loaded. Add any remaining requirement in plain language, such as a sign-in prompt that still appeared during your rehearsal. Keep the note available locally. The purpose is to distinguish what you actually checked from what you only installed or intended to try; a list of optimistic assumptions is less useful once the connection has gone.
Treat local progress and cloud progress separately

Valve's Steam Cloud guidance warns that offline play delays synchronisation and can lead to a conflict when you reconnect. Before leaving, allow any pending synchronisation to finish and confirm that the save you expect loads locally. If you also play on another computer, avoid creating different new progress in the same game without understanding its save handling. Do not assume that a cloud icon is a substitute for checking the actual save. For important progress, consult the game's official instructions about save locations and supported backups before moving files. Save formats and storage locations are game-specific, so a folder path from an unrelated title is not reliable evidence.
Read a synchronisation conflict before choosing

When a conflict appears after reconnection, stop and compare the information shown with the session you want to retain. Check the device, timestamps and the progress you remember making. Do not choose a file simply because one button looks like the normal next step. If the information is ambiguous, preserve the relevant local files where the game's documentation permits and ask official support before overwriting anything. The useful outcome is the intended progress retained and the synchronisation issue resolved, not merely a dismissed warning. Keep your notes until you have opened the game again and confirmed that the expected state is present.
Build a fallback that does not depend on guesswork

A sensible travel library contains more than one title you have actually prepared and checked. Record which games worked offline, the date of the check and any mode that still needed a network connection. This takes less effort than troubleshooting an entire library after departure. If you also want to capture a highlight, test Steam Game Recording and export before the trip. If access to a shared title is uncertain, investigate Steam Families eligibility and copy availability as a separate question. Each check answers one specific problem and leaves the others visible.
